title: Method for organic fluorine determination in gasoline and its components using high-resolution continuum source flame molecular absorption spectrometry with gallium fluoride as a target molecule
author: Kowalewska, Brzezińska, et al.
materials:
Gallium (as GaAA) basic solution, containing 10 000 mg L−1
of Ga: To 5.266 g (± 0.001 g) of GaAA, weighted in a 150 mL glass beaker, 65 mL of xylene should be added, and the content of the beaker should be gently heated on an electric cooker and stirred with a glass rod. After 20 min the beaker should be taken of the cooker and cooled, to add 10 mL of 2-ethylhexanoic acid. Next, the heating of the beaker and mixing of its content should start again and be continued until salt dissolution. The cooled solution should be quantitatively transferred to 100 mL volumetric flask. The obtained solution can show some opalescence, but, should not contain any sediment. It is preferable to use this solution on the day of its preparation.

The volume of 100 mL of the GaAA solution will enable preparation of all solutions needed for analysis of two samples in duplicate, including samples and standard solutions for standard addition calibration, blank, as well as control solutions. In the case of analysis of more samples, more GaAA should be prepared. To spare GaAA, it can be beneficial to determine final mass of the solution, instead of volume. In this way, any calculated as necessary amount of the GaAA can be prepared, without limitation of available volumetric flasks.

Basic solution of fluorine, containing 10,000 mg L−1 of F (as HFB): Approximately 0.301 g (± 0.001 g) of HFB was weighted into a 100 mL Erlemeyer flask and diluted to final mass 50,000 g (± 0.001 g) with xylene.

Intermediate solution of fluorine, containing 1 000 mg L−1 of F (as HFB): Approximately 5.000 g (± 0.001 g) of basic solution of fluorine, containing 10,000 mg L−1 of F (as HFB) was weighted into a 100 mL Erlenmeyer flask and diluted to final mass 50,000 g (± 0.001 g) with xylene.
Blank sample: a sample, which does not contain measurable F content. In the best case blank sample is of the type of the investigated samples.

Working solutions comprise solutions listed below. Blank solution, BL0: a solution containing blank sample, diluted 1:10 v:v in xylene (without GaAA).
Blank solution, BLA: a solution containing blank sample, prepared as investigated samples of type A (with GaAA).
Control solution 1, CS1: a solution containing 100 mg L−1 of F (as HFB) and GaAA in xylene.
Control solution 2, CS2, a solution containing 100 mg L−1 of F (as HFB), GaAA and blank sample (diluted 1:10 v:v) in xylene.
Sample solution of type A: a solution containing the investigated sample (diluted 1:10 v:v) and GaAA, without added F.
Sample solution of type B: a solution containing the investigated sample (diluted 1:10 v:v), GaAA and 50 mg L−1 of added F (as HFB).
Sample solution of type C: a solution containing the investigated sample (diluted 1:10 v:v), GaAA and 100 mg L−1 of added F (as HFB).

The content of Ga in working solutions, quoted above and in Table 1, was equal to 5000 mg L−1, with the exception of BL0. The BL0 solution is used to adjust and control baseline. As the presence of Ga in the solution is not indispensable, it was not added (saving of GaAA).

Solutions A-C of a given sample are for standard addition calibration. The solutions should be prepared in duplicate. Thus, for a given sample of number 1 the working solutions can be labelled as A11, B11, C11, A12, B12 and C12. For each series of samples, two solutions of blank of type BLA should be prepared (BLA1 and BLA2).

steps.title: Prepare GaAA basic solution
steps.instruction: Make a 10 000 mg L⁻¹ gallium solution (GaAA) in xylene.

substeps.instruction: Weigh 5.266 g ± 0.001 g of gallium(III) acetylacetonate (GaAA) into a 150 mL glass beaker.
Heat gently on an electric cooker while stirring with a glass rod for 20 min.
Remove from heat, allow to cool, then add 10 mL of 2‑ethylhexanoic acid.
Re‑heat and stir until the solid is completely dissolved (solution may appear opalescent but must be free of sediment).
Cool the solution and transfer quantitatively to a 100 mL volumetric flask; make up to the mark with xylene.
Use the solution on the day of preparation.

steps.title: Determine required GaAA volume
steps.instruction: Calculate the amount of GaAA solution needed for the planned number of samples (100 mL of the 10 000 mg L⁻¹ GaAA solution suffices for two samples in duplicate, including all standards, blanks and controls).

steps.title: Prepare basic fluorine solution
steps.instruction: Make a 10 000 mg L⁻¹ fluorine stock solution (as HFB) in xylene.

substeps.instruction: Weigh 0.301 g ± 0.001 g of 1‑hydroxy‑2‑fluorobenzene (HFB) into a 100 mL Erlenmeyer flask.
Add xylene and dilute to a final mass of 50 000 g ± 0.001 g (≈50 mL).

steps.title: Prepare intermediate fluorine solution
steps.instruction: Dilute the basic fluorine stock to obtain a 1 000 mg L⁻¹ fluorine solution (as HFB).

substeps.instruction: Weigh 5.000 g ± 0.001 g of the 10 000 mg L⁻¹ fluorine stock solution into a 100 mL Erlenmeyer flask.
Add xylene and dilute to a final mass of 50 000 g ± 0.001 g.

steps.title: Prepare working solutions (Table 1)
steps.instruction: Prepare all calibration and control solutions using the volumes and masses listed in Table 1.

substeps.instruction: Blank solution BL0: pipette 2.5 mL of blank sample, add xylene to a final volume of 25 mL (no GaAA added).
Blank solution BLA: pipette 1.0 mL of blank sample, add 4.4 g of GaAA solution, fill to 10 mL with xylene.
Control solution CS1 (100 mg L⁻¹ F): add 1.1 g of GaAA solution and 2.5 g of intermediate fluorine solution, fill to 25 mL with xylene.
Control solution CS2 (100 mg L⁻¹ F + blank): add 2.5 mL of blank sample, 1.0 g of GaAA solution, 2.5 g of intermediate fluorine solution, fill to 25 mL with xylene.
Sample solution A (no added F): add 1.0 mL of the investigated sample, 4.4 g of GaAA solution, fill to 10 mL with xylene.
Sample solution B (50 mg L⁻¹ added F): add 1.0 mL of the investigated sample, 4.4 g of GaAA solution, 0.5 g of intermediate fluorine solution, fill to 10 mL with xylene.
Sample solution C (100 mg L⁻¹ added F): add 1.0 mL of the investigated sample, 4.4 g of GaAA solution, 1.0 g of intermediate fluorine solution, fill to 10 mL with xylene.

steps.title: Prepare duplicate sets for each sample
steps.instruction: For each gasoline or component sample prepare two independent sets of solutions A, B, C (e.g., A1, B1, C1 and A2, B2, C2) and two blanks of type BLA (BLA1, BLA2).

steps.title: Set up spectrometer and perform reference measurement
steps.instruction: Store the adjusted instrument conditions, then run a reference measurement with pure xylene to set the optical baseline.

steps.title: Check flame stability periodically
steps.instruction: Aspirate the BL0 solution at regular intervals and observe the flame; a lean (more blue) flame indicates blockage of the solution introduction system.

steps.title: Monitor control solution absorbance
steps.instruction: Measure CS1 or CS2 (e.g., between samples or every ten solutions) and verify that its absorbance remains within ±5 % of the initial value.

steps.title: Measure sample and blank solutions
steps.instruction: Aspirate each working solution (A, B, C) in duplicate and record the absorbance at 211.248 nm.

steps.title: Construct standard‑addition calibration
steps.instruction: For each sample plot absorbance versus added fluorine concentration (0, 50, 100 mg L⁻¹) using the duplicate A‑C data, fit a linear regression, and ensure the correlation coefficient (R²) exceeds 0.995.

steps.title: Calculate fluorine content in sample solution
steps.instruction: Extrapolate the regression line to zero absorbance to obtain the fluorine concentration in the undiluted sample solution (type A).

steps.title: Verify repeatability
steps.instruction: Confirm that the two independent determinations for the same sample differ by less than 20 % of their average.

steps.title: Report final concentration
steps.instruction: Average the duplicate results, subtract the blank contribution, multiply by the dilution factor (10 for 1:10 v/v dilution or 4 for 1:4 v/v dilution as used), and round to the nearest 1 mg L⁻¹ for the original gasoline or component sample.

description: The aim of this paper is presentation of a method devoted to organic fluorine determination in gasoline and its components. The development of the method and its scientific background was presented in detail in a paper published alongside this work in Talanta [1]. The method relies on sample dilution in xylene, with addition of necessary reagents and standards and aspiration of the solutions into flame of high-resolution continuous source absorption spectrometer. Simple, low temperature and easy for operation air-acetylene flame is used to decompose organic fluorine compounds as well as gallium(III acetylacetonate, applied as a source of gallium. If fluorine is present in solution, gallium monofluoride is formed in the flame, which is used as a target molecule, absorbing radiation at selected, specific wavelength. The absorption is due to changes of rotational states of the molecule. The measured most sensitive rotational “line” at 211.248 nm belongs to the ∆ν = 0 vibrational transmission within the X1Σ+→C1П electronic transition. As gallium is added in huge and the same amount to all working solutions, the measured absorption by GaF molecule is directly proportional to the fluorine content in the investigated working solutions. Unfortunately, only one compound of Ga, dissoluble in xylene and samples, was available, gallium(III) acetylacetonate. Its dissolution is not easy and should be carried out with care. High resolution continuum source molecular spectrometry, known in its commercial version since the first decade of this century, is widely applied for fluorine determination [2], [3], [4], [5]. However, almost all papers concern electrothermal version with target molecules generated in a graphite furnace (the technique is very sensitive, but slow). What is more, none work is known on determination of fluorine in gasoline or similar materials using both graphite furnace and flame molecular absorption techniques.
